summary.text: Assuming only finitely many failures yields a cutoff beyond which divisibility propagates transitively; Bertrand’s theorem supplies a sufficiently large prime \(p\), and growth estimates give indices \(M\le y\le n-1\) such that \(2p\) lies in the \(y\)-th triangular interval while the \(n\)-th interval lies strictly between \(2p\) and \(3p\). Thus \(p\mid a(y)\) must propagate to \(p\mid a(n)\), but the latter interval contains no multiple of \(p\), so \(p\nmid a(n)\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T_r=\frac{r(r+1)}2\qquad(r\ge 0)
\]
be the triangular numbers. Thus the sequence in question can be written as
\[
a(r)=\prod_{\substack{T_{r-1}<m\le T_r\\m\text{ composite}}}m
\]
for positive integers \(r\). We will prove that there are infinitely many indices \(r>1\) for which \(a(r-1)\nmid a(r)\).

Suppose, for a contradiction, that there are only finitely many such indices. A finite set of natural numbers is bounded, so there is an integer \(M_0\) such that every exceptional index is at most \(M_0\). Put
\[
M=\max(M_0,15).
\]
It follows that
\[
a(k)\mid a(k+1)\qquad\text{for every }k\ge M. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, if \(k\ge M\), then \(k+1>M\ge M_0\), so \(k+1\) is not exceptional; moreover \(k+1>1\), and hence the definition of exceptional index says precisely that \(a(k)\mid a(k+1)\).

We now choose a prime much larger than \(M\). Set
\[
M'=\max(M^2+15,15).
\]
(In fact this maximum is simply \(M^2+15\), but the displayed form makes both bounds \(M'\ge M^2\) and \(M'\ge15\) immediate.) By Bertrand's postulate, applied to the positive integer \(2M'-3\), there is a prime \(p\) satisfying
\[
2M'-3<p\le 2(2M'-3). \tag{2}
\]
Only the lower bound in (2) will be needed. Since \(M'\ge15\), it implies in particular that \(p\ge19\).

The same lower bound also makes \(p\) sufficiently large compared with \(M^2\). Namely,
\[
4p>8M'-12>M'\ge M^2, \tag{3}
\]
where \(8M'-12>M'\) follows from \(M'\ge15\). Consequently
\[
2p>\frac{M(M-1)}2=T_{M-1}. \tag{4}
\]
For example, after multiplying by \(2\), (4) follows from
\(4p>M^2\ge M(M-1)\).

Next, let \(x\) be the least nonnegative integer for which
\[
3p\le T_x. \tag{5}
\]
Such an integer exists because triangular numbers are unbounded. Define
\[
n=x-1.
\]
The minimality of \(x\) gives
\[
T_n<3p\le T_{n+1}, \tag{6}
\]
because \(x=n+1\).

We need a lower bound on \(n\). Since \(p\ge19\), we have \(3p\ge57\). If \(x\le10\), then \(T_x\le T_{10}=55\), contradicting (5). Therefore \(x\ge11\), and hence
\[
n\ge10. \tag{7}
\]

For every \(n\ge10\), the following elementary quadratic inequality holds:
\[
2(n+1)(n+2)\le 3n(n-1). \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, the right side minus the left side is
\[
3n(n-1)-2(n+1)(n+2)=n^2-9n-4,
\]
which is positive at \(n=10\) and increases thereafter. In terms of triangular numbers, (8) is equivalent to
\[
2T_{n+1}\le3T_{n-1}. \tag{9}
\]
Combining \(3p\le T_{n+1}\) from (6) with (9) gives
\[
6p\le2T_{n+1}\le3T_{n-1},
\]
and therefore
\[
2p\le T_{n-1}. \tag{10}
\]
Together, (6) and (10) show that the entire \(n\)-th triangular block lies above \(2p\) and below \(3p\): if
\[
T_{n-1}<m\le T_n,
\]
then
\[
2p<m<3p. \tag{11}
\]
There is no multiple of \(p\) strictly between \(2p\) and \(3p\). Thus no integer in the \(n\)-th block is divisible by \(p\). In particular, none of the composite integers occurring as factors of \(a(n)\) is divisible by \(p\). Since \(p\) is prime, Euclid's lemma says that if \(p\) divides a finite product, then it divides one of its factors. We conclude that
\[
p\nmid a(n). \tag{12}
\]
This conclusion also covers the possibility of an empty product, since a prime does not divide \(1\).

We now construct an earlier block whose product is divisible by \(p\). Let \(y\) be the least nonnegative integer such that
\[
2p\le T_y. \tag{13}
\]
Again, such an integer exists because triangular numbers are unbounded. By minimality,
\[
T_{y-1}<2p\le T_y. \tag{14}
\]
Thus \(2p\) belongs to the \(y\)-th block \((T_{y-1},T_y]\). Since \(p\ge19\), the number \(2p\) is composite: it has the proper divisor \(2\), with \(1<2<2p\). Hence \(2p\) is one of the factors in the defining product for \(a(y)\). It follows that
\[
2p\mid a(y),
\]
and in particular
\[
p\mid a(y). \tag{15}
\]

We next locate \(y\) relative to \(M\) and \(n\). First,
\[
y\ge M. \tag{16}
\]
For if \(y<M\), then \(y\le M-1\). Since triangular numbers are increasing, this would give
\[
T_y\le T_{M-1}<2p
\]
by (4), contradicting (13).

Second,
\[
y\le n-1. \tag{17}
\]
Indeed, (10) says \(2p\le T_{n-1}\), while \(y\) was defined to be the least index whose triangular number is at least \(2p\). Therefore its minimality gives \(y\le n-1\).

Now apply the assumed eventual divisibility (1). From (16), (17), and repeated transitivity of divisibility, we obtain
\[
a(y)\mid a(y+1)\mid\cdots\mid a(n-1)\mid a(n). \tag{18}
\]
More explicitly, every step in this chain has initial index at least \(y\ge M\), so every step follows from (1). Combining (15) with (18) yields
\[
p\mid a(n). \tag{19}
\]
But (19) contradicts (12).

The contradiction arose from assuming that the exceptional set was finite. Therefore the set
\[
\{r\in\mathbb N:r>1\text{ and }a(r-1)\nmid a(r)\}
\]
is infinite. Hence the conjecture that there are only finitely many integers \(n>1\) for which \(a(n-1)\nmid a(n)\) is false.
